summary: Defines SDP semantics for signaling that one media description depends on others for decoding, which is needed when layered or multiple-description coded media is split across different network streams. A receiver can then know which streams to combine.

plainLanguage.summary:
Some video is split into several streams, where one stream is only useful together with another. SDP had no way to say which streams depend on which. This RFC adds that way, so a receiver can tell which streams it needs.

It adds a grouping called DDP and an attribute called depend. The attribute names the other streams that each one has to be decoded with.

questions: what is the sdp depend attribute
what is ddp grouping in sdp
how does sdp signal layered video dependency
what is an operation point in layered coding
subtitle: A way for a session description to say which media streams have to be decoded together.

tldr.problem: A session description can list several media streams of the same type, but SDP had no way to say how they depend on each other, so a receiver could not tell which streams it needed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a grouping semantic called DDP and a new media-level attribute called depend. The attribute names, for each media format, the other media descriptions it must be decoded with, and whether that relationship is layered or multi-descriptive.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can now work out which combination of streams makes a usable picture, which is what layered and multi-description codecs need. The document is a Proposed Standard and applies only with RTP.

today: RFC 5583 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the DDP grouping and the depend attribute in SDP; the media format that motivated it, the RTP payload format for scalable video, is specified in a separate document. The attribute itself was registered with IANA under the SDP attribute and grouping semantics registries.

sections.title: The Gap in Session Description
sections.content:
An SDP session description may contain one or more media descriptions, each identifying a single media stream and each written as one m= line. When more than one m= line carries the same media type, a receiver cannot tell how those media relate to each other.

That matters for coded media that is split across several streams. A Multiple Description Coding (MDC) or layered media bitstream contains, by definition, one or more Media Partitions, each conveyed in its own media stream. The cases of interest here are layered and MDC bitstreams with two or more partitions. Carrying more than one partition in a session is what makes it possible for senders, network elements or receivers to suppress individual partitions and still have useful, if poorer, media quality.

The partitions of any such bitstream have a defined relationship. In layered coding the higher partitions are useless without the lower ones. In MDC coding the partitions are complementary: the more of them a receiver has, the better the quality it can reproduce. This RFC defines an SDP extension that signals such a decoding dependency.

The work was triggered by the standardisation of the RTP payload format for the Scalable Video Coding extension to H.264 / MPEG-4 AVC. While that was being drafted it became clear that the gap in signalling was not specific to SVC but applied to all layered or MDC codecs, so the solution is presented generically. The mechanisms depend on the media transport protocol and apply only with RTP. Grouping media lines of different media types is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Some video is split into several streams, where one stream is only useful together with another. SDP had no way to say which streams depend on which. This RFC adds that way, so a receiver can tell which streams it needs.

sections.title: Media Partition, Operation Point and Dependency
sections.content:
The RFC builds on the SDP definition of a media stream and adds five terms of its own.

  • Media Bitstream: a valid, decodable stream containing all the media partitions generated by the encoder, normally conforming to a media coding standard.
  • Media Partition: a subset of a media bitstream intended for independent transportation. An integer number of partitions forms a bitstream. In layered coding a partition is one or more layers handled as a unit; in MDC coding it is one or more descriptions handled as a unit.
  • Decoding dependency: the class of relationship the partitions have to each other. This document defines two: layered coding and Multiple Description Coding.
  • Layered coding dependency: each partition is only useful when all the partitions it depends on are available, so the dependencies form a directed graph. Normally the more partitions are used, the better the reproduced quality.
  • Multiple Description Coding dependency: N of M partitions are required to form a media bitstream, but there is no hierarchy between them. Some schemes require more than one partition to form an Operation Point.

An Operation Point is a subset of a layered bitstream that includes all the partitions required for reconstruction at a certain point of quality, error resilience or another property, and that includes no other partitions. In MDC coding it is a subset that complies with the coding standard in question.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names the pieces of a split video: a partition is a piece that can travel on its own, and an operation point is the set of pieces that together give a usable picture. A dependency says one piece needs another.

sections.title: Why Layered and Multi-Description Coding Need Signalling
sections.content:
Both kinds of coding share a motivator: adapting the media to the conditions of the network, which means bandwidth, error rates and the connectivity of endpoints in multicast or broadcast situations.

In layered coding the partitions are called layers, and one or more layers may travel in different media streams. A classic use case is receiver-driven layered multicast, where a receiver picks a combination of media streams to match its quality or bit-rate needs. The media formats of the mid 1990s had a single chain of layers: each enhancement layer referred to exactly one layer below it, and the base layer was self-contained, so naming one enhancement layer fully specified the operation point. SDP supported exactly that case, by allowing a range of transport addresses in one media description, where a higher transport address meant a higher layer.

Newer media formats leave that simple chain behind and can implement dependency hierarchies that are at least tree-shaped. Industry has found cases that need them, but SDP cannot express them, so a receiver cannot make an informed decision about which layers to subscribe to. Layered dependencies can also appear in Multi-View Coding, where views are coded against each other to save bits and the partitions, one per view, cannot be decoded on their own.

In the simplest form of MDC each partition is an independent representation of the media, so any one of them decodes to something useful, and decoding more of them together gives better quality, with the best quality when all are present. More complex forms need at least N of M partitions before anything meaningful can be decoded. The RFC covers MDC because it expects such formats to come into practical use and because the signalling solution is much the same as for layered coding.

At the time of writing, no other dependency relationships had been identified that would warrant standardisation, but the mechanism could be extended with new code points for new dependency types, and such a type MUST be documented in an IETF Standards-Track document.
sections.plainLanguage: Splitting a video lets a receiver take only what it can handle, which matters on a slow link or in a multicast session. Older formats put the layers in a straight chain, which SDP could already describe. Newer formats branch out, and SDP needed a way to say so.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content: Dependency signalling is only feasible between media descriptions that have an m= line and carry a media identification attribute, mid, as defined in RFC 3388. All media descriptions grouped under this specification MUST have the same media type. Dependency relations between different media types have to be addressed in other specifications. A media description MUST NOT be part of more than one group of the grouping type defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism works only between media descriptions that carry a mid attribute, and the ones in a group must all be of the same media type.

sections.title: The DDP Group and the depend Attribute
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new grouping semantic, Decoding Dependency, with the token DDP. It associates a media stream, identified by its mid attribute, with a DDP group. Each media stream MUST be composed of an integer number of media partitions and is identified within its media description by a session-unique media format description, which is an RTP payload type number. In a DDP group all media streams MUST have the same type of decoding dependency, as signalled by the depend attribute, and all media streams MUST contain at least one operation point. The group type tells the receiver to handle the media streams of the group according to the depend attribute.

When several codecs are offered, for example in the offer/answer model, the media streams MUST have the same dependency structure whichever media format description is used.

The new media-level attribute is called depend, and its syntax is given in ABNF. A dependency-tag carries a dependency-type and then, for each media description that the dependent format needs, an identification-tag, which is the mid of that description, followed by the fmt values it depends on. There MUST be exactly one dependency-tag per dependent-fmt. The attribute MUST be followed by a sequence of dependent-fmt and dependency-tag fields identifying all the related media format descriptions in all the related media descriptions of the dependent-fmt, and it MAY be used with multicast as well as with unicast transport addresses.

The dependency-type is lay for a layered dependency, which identifies the described media stream as one or more partitions of a layered bitstream, and mdc for a multi-descriptive dependency, which signals that the stream is part of a set of an MDC bitstream. In both cases all the media streams required for decoding the operation point MUST be identified by the identification-tag and fmt-dependency that follow. The values of N and M for an MDC group are not signalled in this context. Where a list of fmt-dependency values is given, any element of the list is enough to satisfy the dependency, at the choice of the decoding entity. Any further dependency type MUST be defined in a Standards-Track document.
sections.plainLanguage: The new attribute sits inside a media description. For each format it lists, it names the other media descriptions the format has to be decoded with, and says whether the relationship is layered or multi-descriptive.

sections.title: Two Worked Examples
sections.content:
The first example has three media descriptions, all of type video, with a layered decoding dependency. Each carries two possible media format descriptions with different encoding parameters, for example a different packetization-mode, for the media subtypes H264 and H264-SVC. The first media description carries two H264 payload types, 96 and 97, and represents the base layer operation point; it is identified by mid:L1. The other two carry H264-SVC payload types, 98 and 99 for mid:L2 and 100 and 101 for mid:L3, and hold enhancements to the base layer and to the first enhancement layer.

The depend attribute shows how the format descriptions depend on each other. Payload type 100 in mid:L3 depends on payload type 96 or 97 of mid:L1. That is an exclusive choice: 100 can be used with 96 or with 97, but one of the two is needed to decode it. Payload type 101 is different: it depends on two media descriptions at once, on payload type 97 of mid:L1 and on payload type 99 of mid:L2, and both are required to decode it.

The second example has three media descriptions with a multi-descriptive decoding dependency, each with a single format description. Payload type 104 in mid:M1 depends on 105 in mid:M2 and on 106 in mid:M3. Under a multi-descriptive dependency, 105 and 106 can be used to improve the decoding of 104, but they are not required for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two worked examples show the attribute in use. In the layered example one payload type needs either of two base formats, and another needs two formats at once. In the multi-description example the other formats improve the picture but are not needed to decode it.

sections.title: Using the New Semantics with SDP Offer/Answer
sections.content:
Backward compatibility in offer/answer is handled as in RFC 3388. A node that does not understand DDP grouping, whether it does not understand line grouping at all or only the DDP semantics, SHOULD answer an offer that contains DDP grouping either with an answer that ignores the grouping attribute or with a refusal, such as 488 Not acceptable here or 606 Not acceptable in SIP.

In the first case, if the offerer still wants to establish communications, it SHOULD generate a new offer with a single media stream that represents an operation point, which in most cases is the base layer of a layered bitstream. It could equally be an operation point made of a set of enhancement layers, as long as they are all in one media stream. In the second case the offerer SHOULD retry with an offer that includes only a single media stream.

An answerer that understands the semantics has to take the depend attribute into account. The offerer decides the number of media streams and the dependency between them; the answerer cannot change the dependency relations. For unicast sessions where the answerer receives media, the answerer MAY remove media operation points, but it MUST use the dependency relations given in the offer when it sends media, and it MAY send using all the operation points in the offer even if it removed some of them. For multicast sessions the answerer MUST accept all operation points and their dependencies or MUST remove the non-accepted ones completely, because a multicast receiver selects which operation points it actually receives.

If the answerer cannot accept one or more offered operation points, or the dependencies of a media stream, it MAY re-invite with an offer that includes the acceptable operation points and dependencies.
sections.plainLanguage: If one side does not understand the new grouping, it can ignore it or refuse the offer, and the other side can then try again with a single stream. The side that answers cannot change the dependencies the offerer set, but it can drop streams it does not want.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security implications of SDP apply.

The RFC points out one new risk: an attacker could manipulate the dependency signalling of a session description and so mislead a receiver or a middlebox. A receiver might try to compose a media bitstream out of several RTP packet streams that does not form an operation point, even though the signalling made it believe it would, with potentially fatal consequences for the decoding process. The recommendation is that the receiver SHOULD perform an integrity check on the SDP and follow the security considerations of SDP, so that only SDP from trusted sources is trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone who can change the session description could make a receiver assemble a set of streams that cannot be decoded together. The receiver is told to check that the description has not been tampered with.

viz.caption: THE TERMS THE RFC ADDS TO SDP

items.title: Media Bitstream
items.text: A decodable stream holding all the partitions the encoder produced.

items.title: Media Partition
items.text: A subset of a bitstream meant to travel on its own.

items.title: Decoding dependency
items.text: The relationship the partitions have to each other.

items.title: Operation Point
items.text: The set of partitions that together reconstruct the media.

items.title: Layered dependency
items.text: A partition is useless without the partitions it depends on.

items.title: MDC dependency
items.text: N of M partitions are needed, with no hierarchy between them.

items.label: Decoding Dependency
items.desc: The SDP grouping semantic that ties media streams together.

items.label: Layered decoding dependency
items.desc: The stream is one or more partitions of a layered bitstream.

items.label: Multi-descriptive decoding dependency
items.desc: The stream is part of a set of an MDC bitstream.

items.label: SDP media-level attribute
items.desc: The attribute that names the media descriptions a format depends on.

data.title: depend-attribute
data.code:
depend-attribute =
       "a=depend:" dependent-fmt SP dependency-tag
          *(";" SP dependent-fmt SP dependency-tag) CRLF

dependency-tag   =
       dependency-type *1( SP identification-tag ":"
       fmt-dependency *("," fmt-dependency ))

dependency-type  = "lay"
                / "mdc"
                / token

dependent-fmt = fmt

fmt-dependency = fmt

a=group:DDP L1 L2 L3
m=video 40000 RTP/AVP 96 97
b=AS:90
a=framerate:15
a=rtpmap:96 H264/90000
a=rtpmap:97 H264/90000
a=mid:L1

b=AS:64
a=framerate:15
a=rtpmap:98 H264-SVC/90000
a=rtpmap:99 H264-SVC/90000
a=mid:L2
a=depend:98 lay L1:96,97; 99 lay L1:97

b=AS:128
a=framerate:30

a=depend:100 lay L1:96,97; 101 lay L1:97 L2:99
